blocks.heading: The weekly parsha and the Belzer Rav's frozen river

paragraphs.text: The Rav opens by saying that the parsha read each Shabbos is bound up with the events of that week. He tells of timber merchants in the days of Rabbi Sholom of Belz who floated logs downriver to the mills. One spring the river stayed frozen past their delivery date, and they came to the Belzer Rav. He asked which parsha the children were learning in cheder, and hearing it was a winter parsha, told them to learn the parsha of the week, and the river would open.

blocks.heading: Wicks unfit for Shabbos, souls lit on Chanukah

paragraphs.text: Vayeshev and Miketz, the Rav continues, carry Chanukah themes. The Gemara in Shabbos allows wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos to be lit on Chanukah, and the sefarim explain that they stand for souls, as in "the soul of man is the lamp of Hashem". Some souls Shabbos cannot kindle, but the light of Chanukah, brought down by the Chashmonaim's mesirus nefesh, can.
For this reason, he explains, the Chanukah lamp stands below ten tefachim, although the Shechinah never descended below ten: on Chanukah it comes down to those who have no strength to rise.

blocks.heading: Why Yehuda and Tamar interrupt Yosef's story

paragraphs.text: The Rav asks why the parsha of Yehuda and Tamar interrupts the story of Yosef's sale. He brings Rashi on Bereishis 39:1: just as Tamar meant it for Heaven, so did Potiphar's wife, who saw through astrology that she would have children from Yosef, though they came from her daughter. He then turns to the Kad HaKemach of Rabbeinu Bachya, noting that the Bnei Yissaschar discusses the same idea.

blocks.heading: The light of Mashiach in the Chanukah lights

paragraphs.text: The Kad HaKemach says that while the Chanukah lights burn, the hidden light of creation, the light of Mashiach, is revealed in them, and eyes purified by Torah and mitzvos can see it. The Rav adds that all the signs show this is the generation of Mashiach, who comes to a very low generation, and the signs are given so that people do teshuvah.

Now the Rav answers his question. In the parsha of Yehuda, Peretz is born, the forefather of David, whom the Jews mention in Lecha Dodi and whose house is blessed in Rus; he is the root of Mashiach ben David. There will be two Mashiachs, ben Yosef first and then ben David, and Potiphar's wife's vision is fulfilled through her daughter Asenath, mother of Ephraim, root of Mashiach ben Yosef.

So both Mashiachs are in this sidra. Both parshiyos open with a descent, "Yehuda went down" and "Yosef was brought down", hinting that the light of Chanukah and of both Mashiachs reaches the lowest generation, the heel.

The two parshiyos show two ways Hashem leads the world. The Rav describes Jewish history, the descent to Mitzrayim, the exiles and the living mesorah of Torah, as a wondrous plan. Sometimes salvation comes through the righteous deeds of tzaddikim; sometimes the wicked, without knowing it, become its cause. Even the sale of Yosef, though the brothers were holy, was not an act of righteousness, yet the salvation came through it.

blocks.heading: Yehuda's desire, Yosef's refusal, and Asenath

paragraphs.text: Mashiach ben David came through Yehuda, whom the Midrash says an angel of desire overpowered; from that came Peretz, root of kingship and of Mashiach. Potiphar's wife told Yosef that Mashiach ben Yosef would come from them, but Yosef answered that he would commit no aveirah to bring Mashiach, refusing her day after day.

The Rav contrasts her with Tamar, who would rather be burned than shame Yehuda, as the Gemara learns. Potiphar's wife, her intention mixed with desire, had Yosef thrown into prison, which led him to Pharaoh's throne and to Asenath, Dinah's daughter, raised by Potiphar's wife and so called her daughter, as the Midrash relates.

blocks.heading: Yosef's test on the idolaters' festival

paragraphs.text: The Rav asks why Rashi tells that the day Yosef came home was the Egyptians' festival. He brings the Rambam that impure thoughts come only to a heart empty of wisdom, and the counsel against them is to learn Torah. That day was the tekufah, when Jews have the custom not to learn. The Gemara in Avodah Zarah tells that Adam HaRishon, seeing the days grow longer, made a festival at the tekufah, which the nations turned into idolatry.

blocks.heading: Chanukah's light on the darkest night

paragraphs.text: So Yosef came to do his accounts, since he could not learn that day, and lacked Torah's protection. Chanukah falls near the tekufah, and the Rav says the sitra achra always imitates kedushah: against the Jews' 25th of Kislev, the nations darken their 25th with their own lights, and even copy the eighth day of Chanukah. But on the darkest night the Jews kindle the light of Mashiach.
